question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical decision.
note: Strong STAR answer with numbers and clear ownership.
answer: In my data structures course project, four of us built a campus room-booking site. My teammate wanted to store bookings in a JSON file because it was quick; I thought two people booking the same room at once would overwrite each other. Instead of arguing in chat, I wrote a 20-line script that fired 50 simultaneous bookings at his version: 9 of the 50 were lost. I showed him the result and proposed SQLite with a unique constraint on room and time slot. He agreed, and I did the migration myself over a weekend. In the final demo we ran the same script and lost zero bookings, and our TA used the script as an example for the next cohort. What I learned is that a small experiment settles a disagreement faster than opinions, and I now try to bring data before I push back.

question: Tell me about a time something you built failed. What happened?
answer: In my second year I wrote a Discord bot that reminded 300 members of our coding club about events. I deployed it on a free host and didn't add any monitoring. Two weeks before our biggest workshop, the host restarted the bot and it silently lost its schedule because I kept reminders in memory. Only 40 people showed up instead of the usual 120. I took responsibility in the club channel, then fixed it properly: reminders moved to a Postgres table, I added a daily health check that pinged me on failure, and I wrote a test that restarts the bot and checks no reminders are lost. Over the next semester the bot sent about 2,000 reminders with no misses, and attendance went back to around 110. The lesson I took is that anything other people depend on needs persistence and monitoring from day one, and I now write down what happens if the process restarts before I ship anything.

question: Walk me through a project you are proud of.
note: Strong project answer: problem first, trade-offs, measured results.
answer: Students in my university's international office kept emailing staff the same visa and enrollment questions, and staff were answering about 200 emails a week by hand. I built a question-answering assistant over the office's 60 policy PDFs. I chunked the documents by section heading rather than fixed size, because answers usually live inside one section, and embedded them with a small open-source model so we didn't send student data to a paid API. I compared plain vector search with hybrid search that also uses keyword matching; hybrid found the right section in 86% of 50 test questions versus 71%, because policy questions often contain exact form names. I wrote the retrieval, the evaluation set and the answer prompt; a friend built the web page. In a two-week pilot, staff said email volume dropped to about 120 a week, and on our test set the assistant cited the correct section 84% of the time. The main weakness is questions that span two policies, which it still answers poorly.

question: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
answer: First, requirements: users create a short link for a long URL and get redirected when they open it; links don't expire unless deleted; and I'll assume 100 million new links a month and a 100 to 1 read to write ratio, so about 40 writes and 4,000 redirects per second on average. Redirects must be fast, under 50 milliseconds. Design: an API service behind a load balancer, a key-value store mapping short code to URL, and a cache in front for hot links. For codes, I'd use a counter-based ID encoded in base62, which gives 7-character codes and no collisions, rather than hashing the URL, which needs collision checks; the trade-off is that sequential codes are guessable, so I'd add a random offset per range. Each app server reserves a range of 1,000 IDs from a central counter so the counter isn't a bottleneck. Reads scale with the cache, since a small fraction of links get most of the traffic, and with read replicas. I'd pick a 301 or 302 redirect depending on whether we need click analytics: 302 lets us count every click but costs more traffic. Analytics events go to a queue so redirects never wait on them.

question: Design the backend for a simple group chat app.
note: Skips requirements entirely: Requirements 2 or below.
answer: I would use WebSockets so messages are pushed instantly. There would be a Node.js server that keeps the socket connections, and messages get saved into MongoDB. When a user sends a message to a group, the server looks up the group members and pushes the message to each connected member. For offline users, messages are stored and delivered when they reconnect. I'd put Redis pub/sub between servers so that if users of the same group are connected to different servers, they still get the message.

question: Design the backend for a simple group chat app.
answer: I'd start by asking how many users and how big groups are; let's say groups up to 100 people and maybe 100,000 users. Users need to send messages, see history and get notifications. I'd have a REST API for history and a WebSocket server for live messages, with Postgres storing messages indexed by group and time. When someone sends a message it is saved first and then pushed to online members, and push notifications go to the others. I think one server could handle this at first, and later we could add more servers.
